title: What are the essential `String` methods every developer should know — `charAt`, `substring`, `indexOf`/`lastIndexOf`, `contains`, `startsWith`/`endsWith`, `replace`/`replaceAll`, `split`, `trim` vs `strip`, `toUpperCase`/`toLowerCase`, `toCharArray`, `getBytes(Charset)`, `compareTo`, `String.format`/`formatted`, and `String.join` — and why is every method non-mutating (returns a new String)?
shortTitle: What are the essential String methods?

s1_definition.profdef: The `String` class is an immutable sequence of characters, so every method that appears to change a string actually returns a brand-new String and leaves the original untouched. The essential methods are `charAt` for a character at an index, `substring` for a slice, `indexOf` and `lastIndexOf` for locating text, `contains`, `startsWith`, and `endsWith` for membership and prefix checks, `replace` for literal replacement and `replaceAll` for regex replacement, `split` for tokenizing on a regex, `trim` and the Unicode-aware `strip` for removing surrounding whitespace, `toUpperCase` and `toLowerCase` for case with a locale, `toCharArray` and `getBytes` for converting to arrays, `compareTo` and `compareToIgnoreCase` for ordering, `String.format` and the instance `formatted` for templating, and `String.join` for concatenating with a delimiter. They are all non-mutating because immutability underlies String's thread safety, pooling, and safe hashing.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a String as a printed statement that the bank treats as a permanent record: once printed you cannot edit it, you can only produce a new corrected copy. So when Rajesh wants an uppercase version of his name or a masked version of his account number, the bank does not scribble on the original; it prints a fresh document and hands that back, while the original stays exactly as it was. The essential methods are the office tools: one to read a single character, one to cut out a portion, one to find where a word appears, one to replace a phrase, one to split a line into fields, one to trim the blank edges, and one to format a neat templated line. Every single tool produces a new document rather than altering the filed original, which is why two clerks can safely share the same filed statement at once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every String method returns a new String and never changes the original, because String is immutable, which is what makes it safe to share, pool, and cache.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `String` class is an immutable sequence of characters, so every method that appears to change a string actually returns a brand-new String and leaves the original untouched. The essential methods are `charAt` for a character at an index, `substring` for a slice, `indexOf` and `lastIndexOf` for locating text, `contains`, `startsWith`, and `endsWith` for membership and prefix checks, `replace` for literal replacement and `replaceAll` for regex replacement, `split` for tokenizing on a regex, `trim` and the Unicode-aware `strip` for removing surrounding whitespace, `toUpperCase` and `toLowerCase` for case with a locale, `toCharArray` and `getBytes` for converting to arrays, `compareTo` and `compareToIgnoreCase` for ordering, `String.format` and the instance `formatted` for templating, and `String.join` for concatenating with a delimiter. They are all non-mutating because immutability underlies String's thread safety, pooling, and safe hashing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a String as a printed statement that the bank treats as a permanent record: once printed you cannot edit it, you can only produce a new corrected copy. So when Rajesh wants an uppercase version of his name or a masked version of his account number, the bank does not scribble on the original; it prints a fresh document and hands that back, while the original stays exactly as it was. The essential methods are the office tools: one to read a single character, one to cut out a portion, one to find where a word appears, one to replace a phrase, one to split a line into fields, one to trim the blank edges, and one to format a neat templated line. Every single tool produces a new document rather than altering the filed original, which is why two clerks can safely share the same filed statement at once.

**One line to remember:** Every String method returns a new String and never changes the original, because String is immutable, which is what makes it safe to share, pool, and cache.

sections.s2_technical:
`charAt(index)` returns the char at a zero-based index and throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` if the index is out of range, for example `"SAV2001".charAt(0)` is the character S. `substring(begin)` and `substring(begin, end)` return a slice from begin inclusive to end exclusive, so `"SAV2001".substring(3)` is "2001" and `"SAV2001".substring(0, 3)` is "SAV". Since Java 7 substring copies the characters rather than sharing the backing array, so it does not pin the whole original in memory.

`indexOf(str)` returns the first index where a substring appears or negative one if absent, and `lastIndexOf(str)` returns the last, for example `"a,b,c".indexOf(',')` is 1. `contains(seq)` returns a boolean membership check, `startsWith(prefix)` and `endsWith(suffix)` test the ends, so `"SAV2001".startsWith("SAV")` is true. These are the everyday search tools and are cheaper than a regex when you only need a literal check.

`replace(target, replacement)` replaces every LITERAL occurrence, so `"1,00,000".replace(",", "")` gives "100000". `replaceAll(regex, replacement)` treats the first argument as a REGEX, so `"a1b2".replaceAll("\\d", "#")` gives "a#b#". A common bug is using replaceAll when you meant a literal replace, because characters like a dot are special in regex. `split(regex)` tokenizes on a regex and by default drops trailing empty strings, while `split(regex, -1)` keeps them, which matters for parsing CSV where trailing empty fields are meaningful.

`trim()` removes leading and trailing characters with a code value at or below the space character, which predates Unicode. `strip()`, added in Java 11, removes leading and trailing Unicode whitespace correctly, so it handles things like a non-breaking space that trim misses, and there are also `stripLeading` and `stripTrailing`. `toUpperCase(Locale)` and `toLowerCase(Locale)` change case, and specifying a locale matters because, for example, the Turkish locale maps the letter i differently, so for machine identifiers you pass Locale.ROOT to avoid locale surprises.

`toCharArray()` returns a fresh char array copy, useful for processing or for passwords you want to wipe. `getBytes(Charset)` encodes the string to bytes with an explicit charset, which you should always specify rather than relying on the platform default. `compareTo(other)` returns a negative, zero, or positive int giving lexicographic order for sorting, and `compareToIgnoreCase` ignores case. `String.format(template, args)` and the instance method `formatted(args)` build a templated string using format specifiers, for example `String.format("Rs.%,.2f", amount)` for a grouped two-decimal number, and `String.join(delimiter, parts)` concatenates an array or iterable with a separator, for example `String.join(",", list)`.

The reason every method is non-mutating is immutability. A String's character content never changes after construction. Any method that seems to modify a string returns a new object. This gives three big benefits. First, thread safety: multiple threads can share a String with no synchronization because no one can change it. Second, the string pool: literal strings are interned and shared, which is only safe because they cannot be mutated. Third, safe hashing and caching: String caches its hash code and can be used as a reliable map key because its hash never changes. A senior engineer adds that this is exactly why heavy concatenation in a loop should use StringBuilder, since each plus on immutable Strings creates a new object, and why security-sensitive secrets prefer char arrays over Strings, because a String lingers immutably in memory and in the pool until garbage collected.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must format and sanitize account data for statements and for a downstream export, and the immutability of String caused confusion that is worth demonstrating.

Problem 1 — a developer called toUpperCase on a customer name expecting the original variable to change, then kept using the original and wondered why it was still lowercase. This is exactly the non-mutating nature of String: the method returns a new string and the original is untouched unless you reassign.

Problem 2 — an account number had to be masked for display, a comma-grouped amount string had to be cleaned to a plain number for parsing, and a raw CSV line had to be split into fields including trailing empty ones. These are exactly the jobs for substring, replace, and split with the keep-empty option, and using the wrong tool, such as replaceAll with a special regex character, produced wrong results.

The fix demonstrates the essential methods used correctly: charAt and substring for masking, replace for cleaning grouping separators, indexOf and startsWith for validation, split with the negative limit for CSV, strip for robust trimming, toUpperCase with Locale.ROOT for a machine-safe code, String.format for a currency line, and String.join to build an output record. It also shows that each call returns a new String by keeping and printing the original alongside the transformed copy.

The code defines an `Account`, a `StatementFormatService` with a `maskAccount` method, a `cleanAmount` method, a `parseCsv` method, and a `formatLine` method. The demo formats a statement line for Rajesh and shows the original strings remain unchanged after every transformation.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's name in lowercase "rajesh kumar"; the account id SAV2001; a grouped amount string "10,00,000.00"; a CSV line with trailing empty fields; and the balance BigDecimal 1000000.00.

Step 1. The demo reads the name and calls toUpperCase with Locale.ROOT, which returns a new string "RAJESH KUMAR". The original name variable still holds "rajesh kumar", proving the method did not mutate the original. The locale root avoids locale-specific casing surprises.

Step 2. The maskAccount method takes SAV2001, computes the length seven, keeps the last four characters 2001 using substring, and builds three X characters for the first three positions, returning "XXX2001". This uses substring to slice and a builder to assemble, and the input string is untouched.

Step 3. The cleanAmount method calls replace with the literal comma, removing all grouping separators to yield "1000000.00". It deliberately uses replace, not replaceAll, because a literal comma needs no regex and using replaceAll would invite regex mistakes with other inputs.

Step 4. The parseCsv method splits the line on commas with a limit of negative one, which preserves the two trailing empty fields, returning a list of five elements including the two empty strings. With the default split those trailing empties would have been dropped, which would misalign a fixed-schema parser.

Step 5. The formatLine method formats the balance with String.format using a grouped two-decimal currency specifier to produce "Rs.10,00,000.00" style output, then joins the name, the masked account, and the amount with a pipe delimiter using String.join, producing the final record line. Each of these calls returns a new string.

Step 6. The demo logs the original and transformed name together, the masked account, the cleaned amount, the CSV field count and contents, and the final statement line, making it clear that every transformation produced a new String while the originals stayed intact.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 18:47:10 [INFO] original name still = 'rajesh kumar', new upper = 'RAJESH KUMAR'
2026-10-30 18:47:10 [INFO] masked account = XXX2001
2026-10-30 18:47:10 [INFO] cleaned amount = 1000000.00
2026-10-30 18:47:10 [INFO] csv fields (5) = [TXN-1, SAV2001, 45000.00, , ]
2026-10-30 18:47:10 [INFO] statement line = RAJESH KUMAR | XXX2001 | Rs.1,000,000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input strings (IMMUTABLE — never modified in place)
    │
    ├─ "rajesh kumar".toUpperCase(ROOT) ─► NEW "RAJESH KUMAR"
    │        original still "rajesh kumar" proof of immutability
    │
    ├─ maskAccount("SAV2001")
    │        substring(len-4) → "2001"; build "XXX" + "2001" ─► "XXX2001"
    │
    ├─ cleanAmount("10,00,000.00")
    │        .replace(",", "") (literal)   ─► "1000000.00"
    │
    ├─ parseCsv("TXN-1,SAV2001,45000.00,,")
    │        .split(",", -1) (keep empties) ─► [TXN-1, SAV2001, 45000.00, "", ""]
    │
    └─ formatLine(name, id, balance)
             String.format("Rs.%,.2f", balance) ─► "Rs.1,000,000.00"
             String.join(" | ", name, masked, amount)
             ─► "RAJESH KUMAR | XXX2001 | Rs.1,000,000.00"

  Every arrow produces a NEW String; inputs remain unchanged.
```

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │  split(regex, -1) to keep trailing empties for fixed schemas.    │

  indexOf/lastIndexOf: locate.  contains/startsWith/endsWith: membership.
  replace: literal.  replaceAll: regex.  split(regex[,limit]): tokenize.
  trim: <=space only.  strip/stripLeading/stripTrailing: Unicode (J11).
  toUpperCase/toLowerCase(Locale): case.  toCharArray/getBytes(Charset).
  compareTo/compareToIgnoreCase: ordering.  format/formatted: template.
  join(delim, parts): concatenate.   ALL return a NEW String.

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     StatementFormatService   │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  + maskAccount(String):String│  substring + builder
  │  + cleanAmount(String):String│  replace (literal)
  │  + parseCsv(String):List     │  split(",", -1)
  │  + formatLine(...):String    │  format + join
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │ formats
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account            │
  │  - holderName: String        │  immutable
  │  - balance: BigDecimal       │  money
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. name.toUpperCase(ROOT) → NEW string (original intact)
  2. maskAccount("SAV2001") → substring("2001") + "XXX" → "XXX2001"
  3. cleanAmount("10,00,000.00") → replace(",","") → "1000000.00"
  4. parseCsv(line) → split(",", -1) → keeps trailing empties
  5. formatLine → String.format + String.join → final record

sections.s6_takeaway:
The String class is an immutable sequence of characters, so every method that appears to change a string actually returns a brand-new String and leaves the original untouched. The essential methods I use daily are charAt for a character at an index and substring for a slice, indexOf and lastIndexOf to locate text, contains and startsWith and endsWith for membership and prefix checks, replace for literal replacement and replaceAll for regex replacement, split to tokenize on a regex, trim and the Unicode-aware strip to remove surrounding whitespace, toUpperCase and toLowerCase with a locale for case, toCharArray and getBytes with an explicit charset for conversions, compareTo for ordering, String.format and the instance formatted method for templating, and String.join to concatenate with a delimiter.

A few of these have traps I always call out. Replace works on a literal while replaceAll treats its first argument as a regex, so I use replace when I only need to swap a literal like a comma, because a dot or other special character would misbehave in replaceAll. Split drops trailing empty fields by default, so for a fixed-schema CSV I pass a limit of negative one to keep them. Trim only removes characters at or below the space value, while strip, added in Java 11, removes Unicode whitespace correctly. And for machine identifiers I pass Locale root to toUpperCase so I avoid locale surprises like the Turkish letter i.

The reason every String method is non-mutating is immutability, and it gives three big benefits. First, thread safety, because multiple threads can share a String with no synchronization since no one can change it. Second, the string pool, because literals can be safely interned and shared only because they cannot be mutated. Third, safe hashing and caching, because a String caches its hash code and is a reliable map key since its content and hash never change. The practical corollary is that heavy concatenation in a loop should use StringBuilder, since each plus on immutable Strings allocates a new object, and that secrets prefer char arrays, since a String lingers immutably in memory until garbage collected.

In our statement-formatting service at National Bank of India, a developer once called toUpperCase on a customer name and kept using the original variable, confused that it was still lowercase, which is exactly the non-mutating behavior: the method returns a new string and you must reassign. I built the formatter using these methods correctly, masking an account with substring, cleaning a grouped amount with literal replace, splitting a CSV line with a keep-empties limit, formatting the currency with String.format, and assembling the record with String.join, and in each case I relied on the fact that the result is a new String while the inputs remain unchanged, which is also what lets our worker threads share formatted strings safely without any locking.
